transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
The president of Israel has chosen Gadi Isincott to try to form the country's next government.
Neither Isincott nor Benjamin Netanyahu secured a clear majority in last month's election.
NPR's Lauren Freire reports Isincott is facing difficult negotiations to bring together
a governing coalition.
He's a former military chief whose son was an Israeli soldier killed in combat in Gaza.
He is a center-right politician, while Netanyahu is on the far right.
Isincott briefly served in Netanyahu's cabinet after the October 7th Hamas attacks on Israel,
but the two had a falling out.
Isincott founded a new political party, ran against Netanyahu, and now wants to replace
him.
Netanyahu's been Israel's longest-serving prime minister, and he is still the caretaker
prime minister for now.
It's NPR's Lauren Freire reporting from Tel Aviv.
The political negotiations come amid efforts to secure a lasting peace agreement in Gaza.
Poland is observing a national day of mourning after a gunman killed at least six people and
wounded more than a dozen in Krakow.
Terry Schultz reports the suspect is a 24-year-old Polish man who was shot and wounded by police.
Authorities say the man fired an automatic rifle from a car driven into the main market
square of Poland's second-largest city before being apprehended.
Three people were found dead at the home of the gunman two hours away from Krakow.
In a press conference, Polish government officials said it appears the gunman was influenced
by far-right ideology.
During the shooting, he wore military-style camouflage and a helmet and was carrying a
large amount of ammunition and weapons in his car.
Four of the dead are women, and one victim is from the U.K.
At least 15 others were injured.
European Union Foreign Policy Chief Kaya Kalis says the tragic loss of life in the shooting
in Krakow is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland.
For NPR News, I'm Terry Schultz in Brussels.
Homelessness in the United States saw a major drop last year, the largest in more than a
decade.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports it was down for the second year in a row.
The Federal Housing Agency HUD announced the decline of more than 6 percent, and it touted
Trump administration policies, like closing the southern border, as a key factor.
Several cities with big drops had seen an earlier surge of asylum seekers in homeless
shelters.
A separate analysis, commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, also finds a
broad decline, says the group's CEO, Anna Levi.
It's good news that more people are getting housed and that the programs that are funded
by Congress are working.
The Trump administration has tried to overhaul those programs, but has so far been blocked
by courts.
Despite the latest decline, nearly 700,000 people remain without housing.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News.
The president of Ultimate Fighting Championships says he's planning to meet with President
Trump at the White House on Monday.
Trump announced that he offered Dana White the job of White House press secretary.
White, who has not publicly said whether he'll accept, has spoken at the past three Republican
national conventions.
Investors on Wall Street are gearing up for the latest inflation report throughout this
week.
As NPR's Ravi El-Nam reports, the data comes at a time when fears about artificial intelligence
are hitting stocks.
The U.S. is set to report how much consumer prices rose in October at a time when voters
have said they're struggling with the cost of living in the most recent midterm elections.
One thing to note is that there's not going to be a comparison to a year ago because of
a government shutdown that prevented the Labor Department from compiling the report in October
last year.
But investors will be seeing how consumer prices fared last month compared to September to
get a better gauge of how inflation is doing.
The report comes at a time when stock markets are under pressure amid fears about the outlook
for A.I. shares.
Ravi El-Nam, NPR News.
The coming days could bring a clearer picture of the still undecided Senate races in Mississippi
and Alaska.
Democrat Scott Colombe is narrowly ahead of Republican senators Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a slim lead over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
Both races remain too close to call with ballots still being counted.
Democrats have already secured control of the upper chamber.
This is NPR News in Washington.
